title: The Layers of the Atmosphere
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The air around the Earth is not the same all the way up. It forms a series of layers, each with its own temperature, pressure and chemical make-up, and together they make up the atmosphere. The layers are not separated by sharp lines; instead, one gradually merges into the next. Altogether, the atmosphere is roughly a hundred kilometres deep, which sounds a great distance but is about the same as the journey between two neighbouring cities. If the Earth were the size of an apple, the atmosphere would be thinner than the apple's skin.

The lowest layer is the troposphere, which extends from the ground to a height of between eight and sixteen kilometres, depending on the latitude and the season. It is the layer in which we live, and it contains about eighty per cent of the mass of the atmosphere and nearly all of its water vapour. For that reason, almost all weather, including clouds, rain and storms, takes place here. The temperature falls steadily as one climbs, by about six degrees for every thousand metres, which is why mountain tops are cold even in summer.

Above it lies the stratosphere, which reaches to about fifty kilometres. Here the pattern changes, and the temperature begins to rise with height. The reason is the ozone layer, a thin region rich in a form of oxygen called ozone. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and in doing so it warms the air around it. Without this natural shield, the radiation reaching the ground would damage plants and cause skin cancer in humans. Because the stratosphere is calm and has few clouds, passenger jets often fly in its lower part.

The mesosphere comes next, from about fifty to eighty-five kilometres above the ground. It is the coldest part of the atmosphere, with temperatures that can fall to ninety degrees below zero. Although the air here is far too thin to breathe, it is dense enough to stop most meteors, which burn up as they enter it and can be seen from the ground as shooting stars. Scientists find the layer hard to study, since it is too high for aircraft and balloons but too low for satellites, and so it has sometimes been called the ignorosphere.

Beyond the mesosphere lies the thermosphere, which stretches to roughly six hundred kilometres. The air here is extremely thin, but it absorbs powerful radiation from the Sun, so its temperature can exceed a thousand degrees Celsius. A person would not feel hot, however, because there are so few molecules to transfer the heat. The thermosphere is the home of the aurora, the glowing curtains of light seen near the poles, which appear when charged particles from the Sun strike the gases. The International Space Station orbits within this layer.

The last layer is the exosphere, which has no clear upper limit. Its gases are so thin that the molecules rarely collide, and some of the lightest, hydrogen and helium, escape slowly into space. Many satellites orbit in or near this layer. Beyond it, the atmosphere fades into the near-emptiness between the planets. Dr Anita Rao, an atmospheric physicist, explains that the border between the atmosphere and space is a matter of convention, and that the most widely used figure, one hundred kilometres, was chosen because it is a round number.

Human activity is changing the atmosphere in ways that scientists are only beginning to understand. In the 1980s, chemicals used in refrigerators and spray cans were found to be destroying ozone over the Antarctic, and an international agreement, signed in 1987, banned them. The ozone layer has since begun to recover. Carbon dioxide, on the other hand, continues to build up in the lowest layer, where it traps heat, and it also cools the upper layers, which are shrinking slowly as a result. The study of these changes is therefore important for the whole planet.
